title: Discriminator Tables Coupling Distinct Types or Admitting Invalid Variants
pattern: Distinct domain objects are forced into one discriminator table with extensive mutually exclusive nullable fields, or a hierarchy/sum type is stored in such a table without constraints enforcing each variant's required and forbidden fields.
why_bad: Unrelated concepts become coupled through one schema, so changes to one concept's attributes (e.g., adding a middle name to Person) pollute the other's record layout and make validation logic fragile. Absent variant-dependent constraints allow records with missing required subtype data or contradictory combinations, and numerous optional columns make the representation harder to understand; performance effects depend on the database and workload.
detection: Inspect discriminator-driven table mappings and subtype-specific nullable columns. Subcase A: substantial unrelated field sets and persistence coupling between distinct concepts that merely share a few fields. Subcase B: columns logically required by a variant are nullable and invalid variant combinations are writable because variant-dependent constraints are missing. Nullable columns and a discriminator alone do not establish either defect.
counterexample: Small, low-complexity tables with nearly all fields shared, or hierarchies with very few subtype-only columns, can be appropriate—especially when query performance justifies the single table and separation provides no logical benefit. A well-constrained single-table design may validly encode variants; it is not structurally incapable of enforcing their invariants.
source: Martin Fowler, *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*, "Single Table Inheritance", p. 278.; Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture, "Single Table Inheritance" [819, 822, 823, 824]
